choices.explanation: GuardDuty identifies suspicious behavior and raises findings; it does not supply the Shield Advanced protection and response capabilities for a large-scale DDoS attack on the load balancer.

choices.solution: Enable Amazon Inspector on the EC2 instances.
choices.explanation: Inspector identifies software vulnerabilities and exposure. It is not a DDoS traffic-mitigation service.

choices.solution: Enable AWS Shield and assign Amazon Route 53 to it.
choices.explanation: The application's DNS is hosted by a third party, so a Route 53 resource is not the application's exposed endpoint in this design. Protecting the actual ELB with Shield Advanced addresses the stated architecture.

choices.solution: Enable AWS Shield Advanced and assign the ELB to it.
choices.explanation: AWS Shield Advanced provides expanded DDoS attack protection for your Amazon EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, and AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerators.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has thousands of edge devices that collectively generate 1 TB of status alerts each day. Each alert is approximately 2 KB in size.

A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to ingest and store the alerts for future analysis. The company wants a highly available solution.

However, the company needs to minimize costs and does not want to manage additional infrastructure. Additionally, the company wants to keep 14 days of data available for immediate analysis and archive any data older than 14 days.

What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon S3 bucket.

Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.
choices.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed service that can capture, transform, and deliver streaming data into storage systems or analytics tools, making it an ideal solution for ingesting and storing status alerts. In this solution, the Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream ingests the alerts and delivers them to an S3 bucket, which is a cost-effective storage solution.

An S3 Lifecycle configuration is set up to transition the data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days to minimize storage costs.

choices.solution:
Launch Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones and place them behind an Elastic Load Balancer to ingest the alerts. Create a script on the EC2 instances that will store the alerts in an Amazon S3 bucket.

Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition data to Amazon S3 Glacier after 14 days.
choices.explanation: The EC2 ingestion fleet and storage script require server provisioning, patching, scaling, and maintenance. This conflicts with the requirement not to manage additional infrastructure.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream to ingest the alerts. Configure the Kinesis Data Firehose stream to deliver the alerts to an Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster.

Set up the Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) cluster to take manual snapshots every day and delete data from the cluster that is older than 14 days.
choices.explanation: An OpenSearch cluster adds an unnecessary search system and capacity management. Manual daily snapshots also fail the goal of a simple automated archival lifecycle.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue to ingest the alerts, and set the message retention period to 14 days. Configure consumers to poll the SQS queue, check the age of the message, and analyze the message data as needed.

If the message is 14 days old, the consumer should copy the message to an Amazon S3 bucket and delete the message from the SQS queue.
choices.explanation: SQS is a message buffer, not a queryable historical data store. Messages expire at the retention limit, and custom consumers must race expiration to archive them and implement their own analysis pipeline.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company's application integrates with multiple software-as-a-service (SaaS) sources for data collection. The company runs Amazon EC2 instances to receive the data and to upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket for analysis.

The same EC2 instance that receives and uploads the data also sends a notification to the user when an upload is complete. The company has noticed slow application performance and wants to improve the performance as much as possible.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution: Create an Auto Scaling group so that EC2 instances can scale out. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.
choices.explanation: Scaling EC2 and moving notifications to SNS can improve throughput, but the team still operates ingestion servers and custom SaaS integrations. AppFlow removes more of that operational work.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon AppFlow flow to transfer data between each SaaS source and the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 event notification to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.
choices.explanation:
Amazon AppFlow is a fully-managed integration service that enables you to securely exchange data between software as a service (SaaS) applications, such as Salesforce, and AWS services, such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift. The use of Appflow helps to remove the ec2 as the middle layer which slows down the process of data transmission and introduce an additional variable.

Appflow is also a fully managed AWS service, thus reducing the operational overhead.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule for each SaaS source to send output data. Configure the S3 bucket as the rule's target.

Create a second EventBridge (Cloud Watch Events) rule to send events when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as the second rule's target.
choices.explanation: A regular EventBridge rule cannot use an S3 bucket as the direct target proposed here. Event routing also does not itself perform the bulk SaaS-to-S3 transfer provided by AppFlow.

choices.solution:
Create a Docker container to use instead of an EC2 instance. Host the containerized application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).

Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to send events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when the upload to the S3 bucket is complete.
choices.explanation: Moving the application into a container does not remove its custom integration work. Container Insights monitors workloads; it does not itself emit an S3 upload-completion notification as proposed.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has a data ingestion workflow that consists of the following:
* An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications about new data deliveries
* An AWS Lambda function to process the data and record metadata The company observes that the ingestion workflow fails occasionally because of network connectivity issues. When such a failure occurs, the Lambda function does not ingest the corresponding data unless the company manually reruns the job.

Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to ensure that the Lambda function ingests all data in the future? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Deploy the Lambda function in multiple Availability Zones.
choices.explanation: Lambda already operates across multiple Availability Zones as a managed service. Choosing more AZs does not add the missing durable work buffer for failed ingestion attempts.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue, and subscribe it to the SNS topic.
choices.explanation: An SQS subscription buffers SNS notifications durably while the downstream system is unavailable.

choices.solution: Increase the CPU and memory that are allocated to the Lambda function.
choices.explanation: More CPU and memory can improve function execution, but they do not preserve messages that need retry after a connectivity failure.

choices.solution: Increase provisioned throughput for the Lambda function.
choices.explanation: Lambda uses concurrency controls rather than the proposed provisioned-throughput setting. Increasing execution capacity does not replace a durable queue with retryable pending work.

choices.solution: Modify the Lambda function to read from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue.
choices.explanation: A Lambda event source mapping processes queued notifications and retries failures, decoupling ingestion from delivery.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company needs guaranteed Amazon EC2 capacity in three specific Availability Zones in a specific AWS Region for an upcoming event that will last 1 week.

What should the company do to guarantee the EC2 capacity?

choices.solution: Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region needed.
choices.explanation: Regional Reserved Instances provide a billing discount but do not reserve capacity in the three specific Availability Zones.

choices.solution: Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation that specifies the Region needed.
choices.explanation: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation is scoped to a particular Availability Zone, not the Region as a whole. The requirement spans three AZs and needs one reservation in each.

choices.solution: Purchase Reserved Instances that specify the Region and three Availability Zones needed.
choices.explanation: Zonal Reserved Instances can reserve capacity, but require a one-year or three-year commitment. That commitment is unnecessarily long for this one-week event compared with cancellable On-Demand Capacity Reservations.

choices.solution: Create separate On-Demand Capacity Reservations in each of the three required Availability Zones in the specified Region.
choices.explanation: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation reserves matching EC2 capacity in one Availability Zone. Create one in each required zone and retain it for the event; a single reservation cannot span three zones.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is developing an application that provides order shipping statistics for retrieval by a REST API. The company wants to extract the shipping statistics, organize the data into an easy-to-read HTML format, and send the report to several email addresses at the same time every morning.

Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Configure the application to send the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose.
choices.explanation: Firehose delivers streaming data; it does not schedule REST queries or send formatted email reports.

choices.solution: Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to format the data and to send the report by email.
choices.explanation: SES delivers the report by email; the application or Lambda function prepares the report content.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Glue job to query the application's API for the data.
choices.explanation: A Glue job adds unnecessary ETL infrastructure for a small scheduled REST request.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled event that invokes an AWS Lambda function to query the application's API for the data.
choices.explanation: An EventBridge schedule invokes Lambda to query the application API and generate the report without maintaining a scheduler server.

choices.solution: Store the application data in Amazon S3. Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as an S3 event destination to send the report by email.
choices.explanation: An S3 notification supplies event metadata, not the required formatted daily HTML report.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company hosts more than 300 global websites and applications. The company requires a platform to analyze more than 30 TB of clickstream data each day.

What should a solutions architect do to transmit and process the clickstream data?

choices.solution: Design an AWS Data Pipeline to archive the data to an Amazon S3 bucket and run an Amazon EMR cluster with the data to generate analytics.
choices.explanation: Data Pipeline batch orchestration does not supply the scalable event-ingestion stream required for clickstream collection.

choices.solution: Create an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances to process the data and send it to an Amazon S3 data lake for Amazon Redshift to use for analysis.
choices.explanation: A custom EC2 ingestion fleet introduces server management and scaling instead of using managed streaming ingestion.

choices.solution:
Cache the data to Amazon CloudFront. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

When an object is added to the S3 bucket. run an AWS Lambda function to process the data for analysis.
choices.explanation: CloudFront caches delivered content; it is not a destination for persisting clickstream events.

choices.solution:
Collect the data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit the data to an Amazon S3 data lake.

Load the data in Amazon Redshift for analysis.
choices.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams handles ingestion, Firehose buffers and delivers data to S3, and Redshift provides warehouse analytics. Firehose delivery is near-real-time rather than immediate per-record delivery.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has a website hosted on AWS. The website is behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is configured to handle HTTP and HTTPS separately.

The company wants to forward all requests to the website so that the requests will use HTTPS.

What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

choices.solution: Update the ALB's network ACL to accept only HTTPS traffic.
choices.explanation: Blocking HTTP drops requests instead of redirecting clients to HTTPS.

choices.solution: Create a rule that replaces the HTTP in the URL with HTTPS.
choices.explanation: Replacing URL text alone does not return the HTTP redirect clients need; configure an ALB redirect action.

choices.solution: Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
choices.explanation: An ALB HTTP listener can redirect requests to an HTTPS listener without changing the application servers. Configure a valid certificate on the HTTPS listener.

choices.solution: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer configured to use Server Name Indication (SNI).
choices.explanation: An NLB does not perform HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects; SNI selects TLS certificates rather than redirecting requests.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is deploying a new public web application to AWS. The application will run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).

The application needs to be encrypted at the edge with an SSL/TLS certificate that is issued by an external certificate authority (CA). The certificate must be rotated each year before the certificate expires.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

choices.solution:
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB.

Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.
choices.explanation: An ACM-issued certificate does not satisfy the requirement for issuance by an external CA.

choices.solution:
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue an SSL/TLS certificate. Import the key material from the certificate.

Apply the certificate to the ALUse the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.
choices.explanation: Importing external key material is not part of requesting an ACM-issued certificate; imported certificates lack managed renewal.

choices.solution:
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) Private Certificate Authority to issue an SSL/TLS certificate from the root CA. Apply the certificate to the ALB.

Use the managed renewal feature to automatically rotate the certificate.
choices.explanation: A private CA certificate is not the required externally issued, publicly trusted certificate.

choices.solution:
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to import an SSL/TLS certificate. Apply the certificate to the ALB.

Use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send a notification when the certificate is nearing expiration. Rotate the certificate manually.
choices.explanation: Import the third-party certificate into ACM and attach it to the ALB. Imported certificates are not automatically renewed by ACM; monitor approaching expiration with EventBridge and replace them manually.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs its infrastructure on AWS and has a registered base of 700,000 users for its document management application. The company intends to create a product that converts large .pdf files to .jpg image files.

The .pdf files average 5 MB in size. The company needs to store the original files and the converted files.

A solutions architect must design a scalable solution to accommodate demand that will grow rapidly over time.

Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

choices.solution: Save the .pdf files to Amazon S3. Configure an S3 PUT event to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in Amazon S3.
choices.explanation: S3 object-created notifications invoke Lambda promptly. Lambda converts the PDF and writes the JPEG back to S3; filter prefixes or suffixes to avoid recursively triggering on its own outputs.

choices.solution: Save the .pdf files to Amazon DynamoDUse the DynamoDB Streams feature to invoke an AWS Lambda function to convert the files to .jpg format and store them back in DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: A 5 MB PDF exceeds DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit.

choices.solution:
Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the files to .jpg format.

Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.
choices.explanation: EC2 conversion fleets add idle compute and maintenance costs; independent EBS volumes also complicate shared storage.

choices.solution:
Upload the .pdf files to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application that includes Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) storage, and an Auto Scaling group. Use a program in the EC2 instances to convert the file to .jpg format.

Save the .pdf files and the .jpg files in the EBS store.
choices.explanation: This adds container/server management, and the option still saves outputs to EBS instead of its proposed shared EFS.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company hosts an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue, writes to an Amazon RDS table, and deletes the message from the queue.

Occasional duplicate records are found in the RDS table. The SQS queue does not contain any duplicate messages.

What should a solutions architect do to ensure messages are being processed once only?

choices.solution: Use the CreateQueue API call to create a new queue.
choices.explanation: Creating another queue does not fix messages becoming visible before processing finishes.

choices.solution: Use the AddPermission API call to add appropriate permissions.
choices.explanation: Queue permissions control access, not concurrent delivery of an in-flight message.

choices.solution: Use the ReceiveMessage API call to set an appropriate wait time.
choices.explanation: Long polling controls empty receive requests, not the visibility timeout protecting an in-flight message.

choices.solution: Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API call to increase the visibility timeout.
choices.explanation: Extend message visibility while processing and delete the message only after success. This prevents a long-running task from making the message visible too early, but standard SQS queues still provide at-least-once delivery; consumers must be idempotent.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is running a business-critical web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group.

The application uses an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database that is deployed in a single Availability Zone. The company wants the application to be highly available with minimum downtime and minimum loss of data.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

choices.solution:
Place the EC2 instances in different AWS Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 health checks to redirect traffic.

Use Aurora PostgreSQL Cross- Region Replication.
choices.explanation: Cross-Region application and database recovery adds complexity beyond a multi-AZ design within one Region.

choices.solution:
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple Availability Zones. Configure the database as Multi-AZ.

Configure an Amazon RDS Proxy instance for the database.
choices.explanation: A Multi-AZ application group and Aurora Replica in another zone provide failover at both tiers. RDS Proxy pools connections and helps applications reconnect during database failover; it does not replace database redundancy.

choices.solution:
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use one Availability Zone. Generate hourly snapshots of the database.

Recover the database from the snapshots in the event of a failure.
choices.explanation: A single AZ remains a failure point; hourly snapshots allow data loss and require restoration downtime.

choices.solution:
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use multiple AWS Regions. Write the data from the application to Amazon S3.

Use S3 Event Notifications to launch an AWS Lambda function to write the data to the database.
choices.explanation: An Auto Scaling group is Regional; an S3-to-Lambda database-write pipeline also adds unnecessary failure modes.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company's HTTP application is behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB). The NLB's target group is configured to use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with multiple EC2 instances that run the web service.

The company notices that the NLB is not detecting HTTP errors for the application. These errors require a manual restart of the EC2 instances that run the web service.

The company needs to improve the application's availability without writing custom scripts or code.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Enable HTTP health checks on the NLB, supplying the URL of the company's application.
choices.explanation: NLB HTTP health checks can detect errors, but this option omits automatic replacement of unhealthy instances.

choices.solution: Add a cron job to the EC2 instances to check the local application's logs once each minute. If HTTP errors are detected. the application will restart.
choices.explanation: A cron-based restart script violates the requirement to avoid custom scripts or code.

choices.solution:
Replace the NLB with an Application Load Balancer. Enable HTTP health checks by supplying the URL of the company's application.

Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances.
choices.explanation:
An ALB supports HTTP-aware health checks and removes unhealthy targets from routing. Enable Elastic Load Balancing health checks on the Auto Scaling group so unhealthy instances are also replaced.

NLBs can support HTTP health checks too, so an NLB is not intrinsically unable to detect HTTP failures.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon Cloud Watch alarm that monitors the UnhealthyHostCount metric for the NLB. Configure an Auto Scaling action to replace unhealthy instances when the alarm is in the ALARM state.
choices.explanation: An alarm on TCP-based unhealthy-host results cannot detect HTTP failures that the NLB is missing.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs a shopping application that uses Amazon DynamoDB to store customer information. In case of data corruption, a solutions architect needs to design a solution that meets a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour.

What should the solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Configure DynamoDB global tables. For RPO recovery, point the application to a different AWS Region.
choices.explanation: Global tables replicate corrupt writes too; switching Regions does not recover an earlier uncorrupted state.

choices.solution: Configure DynamoDB point-in-time recovery. For RPO recovery, restore to the desired point in time.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery restores a new table to a selected time within its configured recovery window, with second-level recovery points. Restore duration depends on table size and indexes, so a one-hour RTO must be tested rather than assumed.

choices.solution: Export the DynamoDB data to Amazon S3 Glacier on a daily basis. For RPO recovery, import the data from S3 Glacier to DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: Daily exports cannot meet a 15-minute RPO; Glacier restoration also delays recovery.

choices.solution: Schedule Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots for the DynamoDB table every 15 minutes. For RPO recovery, restore the DynamoDB table by using the EBS snapshot.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB tables are not customer-managed EBS volumes and cannot be recovered using EBS snapshots.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company wants to move a multi-tiered application from on premises to the AWS Cloud to improve the application's performance. The application consists of application tiers that communicate with each other by way of RESTful services.

Transactions are dropped when one tier becomes overloaded. A solutions architect must design a solution that resolves these issues and modernizes the application.

Which solution meets these requirements and is the MOST operationally efficient?

choices.solution: Use Amazon API Gateway and direct transactions to the AWS Lambda functions as the application layer. Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) as the communication layer between application services.
choices.explanation: API Gateway and Lambda provide managed API processing, while SQS durably buffers inter-service work so an overloaded consumer does not cause dropped transactions.

choices.solution: Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to analyze the application performance history to determine the servers' peak utilization during the performance failures. Increase the size of the application server's Amazon EC2 instances to meet the peak requirements.
choices.explanation: Larger instances do not buffer transactions or decouple tiers when a downstream service becomes overloaded.

choices.solution: Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to handle the messaging between application servers running on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the SNS queue length and scale up and down as required.
choices.explanation: SNS does not expose a work-queue backlog to scale against; published-message count is not outstanding work.

choices.solution: Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to handle the messaging between application servers running on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the SQS queue length and scale up when communication failures are detected.
choices.explanation: SQS helps buffering, but EC2 fleets require more administration than managed API Gateway and Lambda.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A solutions architect is designing the cloud architecture for a new application being deployed on AWS. The process should run in parallel while adding and removing application nodes as needed based on the number of jobs to be processed.

The processor application is stateless. The solutions architect must ensure that the application is loosely coupled and the job items are durably stored.

Which design should the solutions architect use?

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon SNS topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application.

Create a launch configuration that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch configuration.

Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on CPU usage.
choices.explanation: SNS is not the durable pending-job queue required here, and CPU does not measure backlog.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon SQS queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application.

Create a launch configuration that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch configuration.

Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on network usage.
choices.explanation: Network utilization can vary independently of pending jobs; queue depth directly measures the required scaling workload.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon SQS queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application.

Create a launch template that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch template.

Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on the number of items in the SQS queue.
choices.explanation: SQS retains pending jobs independently of the worker fleet. Auto Scaling adds and removes stateless workers as backlog changes; backlog per instance is preferable to raw queue depth for target tracking.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon SNS topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that consists of the processor application.

Create a launch template that uses the AMI. Create an Auto Scaling group using the launch template.

Set the scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to add and remove nodes based on the number of messages published to the SNS topic.
choices.explanation: SNS publish count measures incoming events, not durably queued unfinished jobs.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company's dynamic website is hosted using on-premises servers in the United States. The company is launching its product in Europe, and it wants to optimize site loading times for new European users.

The site's backend must remain in the United States. The product is being launched in a few days, and an immediate solution is needed.

What should the solutions architect recommend?

choices.solution: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance in us-east-1 and migrate the site to it.
choices.explanation: Migrating to another US origin does not add nearby European edge delivery and consumes launch time.

choices.solution: Move the website to Amazon S3. Use Cross-Region Replication between Regions.
choices.explanation: S3 cannot run the dynamic website backend, which must remain on premises.

choices.solution: Use Amazon CloudFront with a custom origin pointing to the on-premises servers.
choices.explanation: CloudFront supports an HTTPS custom origin on premises, serving content from edge locations while keeping the backend in the United States.

choices.solution: Use an Amazon Route 53 geoproximity routing policy pointing to on-premises servers.
choices.explanation: Changing DNS routing to the same US servers does not add caching or shorten the origin network path.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has a production web application in which users upload documents through a web interface or a mobile app. According to a new regulatory requirement. new documents cannot be modified or deleted after they are stored.

What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

choices.solution: Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning and S3 Object Lock enabled.
choices.explanation: S3 Object Lock protects object versions against permanent deletion and alteration during retention. Use compliance mode for non-bypassable regulatory retention and apply the required retention period.

choices.solution: Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to archive the documents periodically.
choices.explanation: Lifecycle archiving changes storage class but does not prohibit modification or deletion.

choices.solution: Store the uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure an ACL to restrict all access to read-only.
choices.explanation: ACL permissions can be changed and do not enforce immutable object retention.

choices.solution: Store the uploaded documents on an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Access the data by mounting the volume in read- only mode.
choices.explanation: A read-only client mount can be remounted writable; it is not a storage-enforced WORM retention policy.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company hosts an application on AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by an Amazon API Gateway API. The Lambda functions save customer data to an Amazon Aurora MySQL database.

Whenever the company upgrades the database, the Lambda functions fail to establish database connections until the upgrade is complete. The result is that customer data is not recorded for some of the event.

A solutions architect needs to design a solution that stores customer data that is created during database upgrades.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Provision an Amazon RDS proxy to sit between the Lambda functions and the database. Configure the Lambda functions to connect to the RDS proxy.
choices.explanation: RDS Proxy manages connections and failover, but does not durably queue writes throughout database unavailability.

choices.solution: Increase the run time of the Lambda functions to the maximum. Create a retry mechanism in the code that stores the customer data in the database.
choices.explanation: Retries are bounded by Lambda's execution timeout and do not durably preserve data beyond an invocation.

choices.solution: Persist the customer data to Lambda local storage. Configure new Lambda functions to scan the local storage to save the customer data to the database.
choices.explanation: Lambda local storage is ephemeral and isolated per execution environment; another function cannot scan it reliably.

choices.solution: Store the customer data in an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Create a new Lambda function that polls the queue and stores the customer data in the database.
choices.explanation: SQS retains customer events while the database is unavailable. A separate Lambda consumer retries database writes after upgrades; make writes idempotent because messages may be delivered again.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A survey company has gathered data for several years from areas in the United States. The company hosts the data in an Amazon S3 bucket that is 3 TB in size and growing.

The company has started to share the data with a European marketing firm that has S3 buckets. The company wants to ensure that its data transfer costs remain as low as possible.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Configure the Requester Pays feature on the company's S3 bucket.
choices.explanation: With Requester Pays, the requesting AWS account pays the request and data-download costs instead. The original company still pays for storing the 3 TB in S3.

choices.solution: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication from the company's S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.
choices.explanation: Replication incurs cross-Region transfer charges to the source bucket owner rather than shifting download costs.

choices.solution: Configure cross-account access for the marketing firm so that the marketing firm has access to the company's S3 bucket.
choices.explanation: Cross-account permission grants access but leaves normal request and download billing with the bucket owner.

choices.solution: Configure the company's S3 bucket to use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Sync the S3 bucket to one of the marketing firm's S3 buckets.
choices.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering reduces storage costs, not the source owner's cross-Region transfer costs for synchronization.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is using a SQL database to store movie data that is publicly accessible. The database runs on an Amazon RDS Single-AZ DB instance.

A script runs queries at random intervals each day to record the number of new movies that have been added to the database. The script must report a final total during business hours.

The company's development team notices that the database performance is inadequate for development tasks when the script is running. A solutions architect must recommend a solution to resolve this issue.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution: Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ deployment.
choices.explanation: A conventional Multi-AZ standby does not serve the script's read queries to offload the primary.

choices.solution: Create a read replica of the database. Configure the script to query only the read replica.
choices.explanation: A read replica moves the reporting script's read workload off the primary instance. It is asynchronous, so allow for replica lag in the report.

choices.solution: Instruct the development team to manually export the entries in the database at the end of each day.
choices.explanation: A manual end-of-day export misses the business-hours reporting deadline and adds operational work.

choices.solution: Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache the common queries that the script runs against the database.
choices.explanation: A cache requires application integration and invalidation; a read replica directly offloads the existing SQL workload.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs an on-premises application that is powered by a MySQL database. The company is migrating the application to AWS to increase the application's elasticity and availability.

The current architecture shows heavy read activity on the database during times of normal operation. Every 4 hours, the company's development team pulls a full export of the production database to populate a database in the staging environment.

During this period, users experience unacceptable application latency. The development team is unable to use the staging environment until the procedure completes.

A solutions architect must recommend replacement architecture that alleviates the application latency issue. The replacement architecture also must give the development team the ability to continue using the staging environment without delay.

Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.solution: Use Amazon Aurora MySQL with Multi-AZ Aurora Replicas for production. Populate the staging database by implementing a backup and restore process that uses the mysqldump utility.
choices.explanation: mysqldump still reads and copies the full database, preserving the latency and staging-refresh delay.

choices.solution: Use Amazon Aurora MySQL with Multi-AZ Aurora Replicas for production. Use database cloning to create the staging database on-demand.
choices.explanation: Aurora replicas handle read workloads, and Aurora cloning initially shares storage pages through copy-on-write. The staging clone remains independent without waiting for a full logical export.

choices.solution: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ deployment and read replicas for production. Use the standby instance for the staging database.
choices.explanation: A conventional RDS Multi-AZ standby is not an independently accessible writable staging database.

choices.solution: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ deployment and read replicas for production. Populate the staging database by implementing a backup and restore process that uses the mysqldump utility.
choices.explanation: A full dump-and-restore still delays staging access and adds database-export load.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is designing an application where users upload small files into Amazon S3. After a user uploads a file, the file requires one-time simple processing to transform the data and save the data in JSON format for later analysis.

Each file must be processed as quickly as possible after it is uploaded. Demand will vary.

On some days, users will upload a high number of files. On other days, users will upload a few files or no files.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution:
Configure Amazon EMR to read text files from Amazon S3. Run processing scripts to transform the data.

Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.
choices.explanation: An EMR cluster and Aurora database add operational and idle-capacity overhead for tiny intermittent jobs.

choices.solution:
Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use Amazon EC2 instances to read from the queue and process the data.

Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: EC2 queue consumers require server scaling and patching rather than execution only when work exists.

choices.solution:
Configure Amazon S3 to send an event notification to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use an AWS Lambda function to read from the queue and process the data.

Store the resulting JSON file in Amazon DynamoDB.
choices.explanation: S3 events enqueue work in SQS and Lambda scales processing with demand without managing workers. DynamoDB stores the transformed JSON as document data; use S3 instead if a literal JSON file object is required.

choices.solution:
Configure Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to send an event to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams when a new file is uploaded. Use an AWS Lambda function to consume the event from the stream and process the data.

Store the resulting JSON file in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.
choices.explanation: Kinesis and Aurora introduce extra infrastructure for a simple one-time per-file transformation.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
An application allows users at a company's headquarters to access product data. The product data is stored in an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance.

The operations team has isolated an application performance slowdown and wants to separate read traffic from write traffic. A solutions architect needs to optimize the application's performance quickly.

What should the solutions architect recommend?

choices.solution: Change the existing database to a Multi-AZ deployment. Serve the read requests from the primary Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: Reads served by the primary remain on the same instance as writes; Multi-AZ alone does not offload them.

choices.solution: Change the existing database to a Multi-AZ deployment. Serve the read requests from the secondary Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: A conventional Multi-AZ standby cannot serve application read traffic.

choices.solution: Create read replicas for the database. Configure the read replicas with half of the compute and storage resources as the source database.
choices.explanation: Undersized replicas can lag and become a new performance bottleneck under the existing read workload.

choices.solution: Create read replicas for the database. Configure the read replicas with the same compute and storage resources as the source database.
choices.explanation: Read replicas offload eligible reads from the writer. The application must route reads to the replica endpoints and tolerate asynchronous replication lag.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
An image-processing company has a web application that users use to upload images. The application uploads the images into an Amazon S3 bucket.

The company has set up S3 event notifications to publish the object creation events to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue. The SQS queue serves as the event source for an AWS Lambda function that processes the images and sends the results to users through email.

Users report that they are receiving multiple email messages for every uploaded image. A solutions architect determines that SQS messages are invoking the Lambda function more than once, resulting in multiple email messages.

What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution: Set up long polling in the SQS queue by increasing the ReceiveMessage wait time to 30 seconds.
choices.explanation: Long polling does not prevent redelivery; SQS also limits ReceiveMessage wait time to 20 seconds.

choices.solution: Change the SQS standard queue to an SQS FIFO queue. Use the message deduplication ID to discard duplicate messages.
choices.explanation: S3 event notifications cannot directly target FIFO queues, and FIFO alone does not make Lambda side effects idempotent.

choices.solution: Set the SQS visibility timeout to at least six times the Lambda function timeout, plus the maximum batching window. Make the function idempotent to tolerate redelivery.
choices.explanation:
A sufficient visibility timeout prevents messages from reappearing while the first Lambda invocation is still running or retrying. AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout plus the batching window.

SQS and Lambda still allow duplicate delivery, so email processing must be idempotent.

choices.solution: Modify the Lambda function to delete each message from the SQS queue immediately after the message is read before processing.
choices.explanation: Deleting before successful processing loses the work if processing subsequently fails.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A solutions architect must design a highly available infrastructure for a website. The website is powered by Windows web servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances.

The solutions architect must implement a solution that can mitigate a large-scale DDoS attack that originates from thousands of IP addresses. Downtime is not acceptable for the website.

Which actions should the solutions architect take to protect the website from such an attack? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Use AWS Shield Advanced to stop the DDoS attack.
choices.explanation: Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS protection and response support for eligible protected resources.

choices.solution: Configure Amazon GuardDuty to automatically block the attackers.
choices.explanation: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity but does not itself absorb or block a volumetric DDoS attack.

choices.solution: Configure the website to use Amazon CloudFront for both static and dynamic content.
choices.explanation: CloudFront distributes static and dynamic HTTP content through edge locations, helping absorb attacks and reduce load on the origin.

choices.solution: Use an AWS Lambda function to automatically add attacker IP addresses to VPC network ACLs.
choices.explanation: Adding individual attacker addresses to network ACLs is reactive and constrained by rule limits; thousands of changing addresses make this unsuitable.

choices.solution: Use EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy that is set to 80% CPU utilization.
choices.explanation: Adding Spot capacity does not filter attack traffic, and interruptions make it unsuitable as the primary availability protection.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A bicycle sharing company is developing a multi-tier architecture to track the location of its bicycles during peak operating hours. The company wants to use these data points in its existing analytics platform.

A solutions architect must determine the most viable multi-tier option to support this architecture. The data points must be accessible from the REST API.

Which action meets these requirements for storing and retrieving location data?

choices.solution: Use Amazon Athena with Amazon S3.
choices.explanation: Athena queries data in S3 for analysis; it is not the REST endpoint and transactional backend for storing and retrieving bicycle locations.

choices.solution: Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda.
choices.explanation: API Gateway exposes a REST API and Lambda implements reads and writes to the location data store. Kinesis analytics processes streams but is not a REST-accessible record store; add the required persistent data store to the implementation.

choices.solution: Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon Redshift.
choices.explanation: QuickSight and Redshift provide analytics and visualization, not the required location-management REST API.

choices.solution: Use Amazon API Gateway with Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics.
choices.explanation: Kinesis stream analytics processes event streams; it does not provide the requested REST storage and retrieval workflow.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has an automobile sales website that stores its listings in a database on Amazon RDS. When an automobile is sold, the listing needs to be removed from the website and the data must be sent to multiple target systems.

Which design should a solutions architect recommend?

choices.solution: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered when the database on Amazon RDS is updated to send the information to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue for the targets to consume.
choices.explanation: RDS event notifications do not trigger Lambda for individual table-row updates, and one shared queue distributes messages rather than delivering every event to every consumer.

choices.solution: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered when the database on Amazon RDS is updated to send the information to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue for the targets to consume.
choices.explanation: A single FIFO queue still distributes messages among consumers; it does not fan out each sale to all target systems.

choices.solution: Subscribe to an RDS event notification and send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue fanned out to multiple Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics. Use AWS Lambda functions to update the targets.
choices.explanation: RDS events describe database-instance operations, not individual sales, and placing SNS after a shared queue does not implement the proposed per-subscriber fan-out.

choices.solution: After an automobile sale is committed, have the application publish the sale event to an Amazon SNS topic. Fan out the topic to a separate SQS queue for each target system, and use Lambda consumers to update the targets.
choices.explanation:
SNS fan-out with separate SQS queues gives each target an independent durable copy of the sale event. RDS service event notifications report database operational events, not row changes.

Publish from the application after commit, preferably through a transactional outbox for reliable delivery.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company recently migrated a message processing system to AWS. The system receives messages into an ActiveMQ queue running on an Amazon EC2 instance.

Messages are processed by a consumer application running on Amazon EC2. The consumer application processes the messages and writes results to a MySQL database running on Amazon EC2.

The company wants this application to be highly available with low operational complexity.

Which architecture offers the HIGHEST availability?

choices.solution:
Add a second ActiveMQ server to another Availability Zone. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone.

Replicate the MySQL database to another Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: Self-managed brokers and database instances require the team to configure replication, failover, and maintenance.

choices.solution:
Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone.

Replicate the MySQL database to another Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: Keeping MySQL on EC2 retains the operational burden of database availability and failover.

choices.solution:
Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone.

Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ enabled.
choices.explanation: Two fixed consumer instances do not provide the automatic replacement and capacity management supplied by an Auto Scaling group.

choices.solution:
Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an Auto Scaling group for the consumer EC2 instances across two Availability Zones.

Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ enabled.
choices.explanation: Amazon MQ active/standby ActiveMQ brokers, a Multi-AZ consumer Auto Scaling group, and RDS MySQL Multi-AZ remove the single-instance dependencies while keeping infrastructure managed.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company uses a popular content management system (CMS) for its corporate website. However, the required patching and maintenance are burdensome.

The company is redesigning its website and wants a new solution. The website will be updated four times a year and does not need to have any dynamic content available.

The solution must provide high scalability and enhanced security.

Which combination of changes will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the website to use HTTPS functionality.
choices.explanation: CloudFront provides HTTPS delivery for the static website. S3 website endpoints themselves support only HTTP.

choices.solution: Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website to provide HTTPS functionality.
choices.explanation: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests; it does not provide the website's HTTPS endpoint and certificate termination.

choices.solution: Create and deploy an AWS Lambda function to manage and serve the website content.
choices.explanation: Lambda adds application execution infrastructure that a static S3-hosted site does not need.

choices.solution: Create the new website and an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy the website on the S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled.
choices.explanation: S3 static website hosting serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images without server patching or instance management.

choices.solution: Create the new website. Deploy the website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.
choices.explanation: EC2 instances require patching and server maintenance for a website that can be served directly from S3 and CloudFront.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company stores its application logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group. A new policy requires the company to store all application logs in Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) in near-real time.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution: Configure a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
choices.explanation: Explanation: CloudWatch Logs supports a native subscription filter that streams straight to OpenSearch Service, so routing through Kinesis Data Firehose is an unnecessary extra hop for this requirement.

choices.solution: Create an AWS Lambda function. Use the log group to invoke the function to write the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
choices.explanation: A custom Lambda integration requires implementing and maintaining delivery logic instead of using the supported CloudWatch Logs subscription integration.

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the log group as the delivery streams sources.

Configure Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service) as the delivery stream's destination.
choices.explanation: Firehose does not automatically read a CloudWatch log group; a subscription must forward the records to it.

choices.solution: Install and configure Amazon Kinesis Agent on each application server to deliver the logs to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Configure Kinesis Data Streams to deliver the logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service).
choices.explanation: Retrofitting agents and configuring a separate streaming pipeline adds operational work compared with a log-group subscription.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is building a web-based application running on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. The web application will provide access to a repository of text documents totaling about 900 TB in size.

The company anticipates that the web application will experience periods of high demand. A solutions architect must ensure that the storage component for the text documents can scale to meet the demand of the application at all times.

The company is concerned about the overall cost of the solution.

Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

choices.solution: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
choices.explanation: EBS requires provisioned volumes and attached compute, making it a poor fit for a scalable 900-TB text-object repository.

choices.solution: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
choices.explanation: EFS adds shared-file-system capabilities and cost that simple text-object storage does not require.

choices.solution: Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service)
choices.explanation: OpenSearch maintains search indexes and compute capacity; that is unnecessary expense when the requirement is storage.

choices.solution: Amazon S3
choices.explanation: S3 scales object storage independently of the application instances and stores a large document repository without provisioning file-system or block-volume capacity.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company has implemented a self-managed DNS solution on three Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the us-west- 2 Region. Most of the company's users are located in the United States and Europe.

The company wants to improve the performance and availability of the solution. The company launches and configures three EC2 instances in the eu-west-1 Region and adds the EC2 instances as targets for a new NLB.

Which solution can the company use to route traffic to all the EC2 instances?

choices.solution:
Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the two NLBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution.

Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.
choices.explanation: CloudFront serves HTTP and HTTPS content; it cannot proxy DNS traffic to the DNS servers.

choices.solution:
Create a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Create endpoint groups in us-west-2 and eu-west-1.

Add the two NLBs as endpoints for the endpoint groups.
choices.explanation: endpoints for the endpoint groups. Explanation: | Option | Why eliminated | | ------ | ----------------------------------- | | A | CloudFront doesn't support DNS | | B | OK Correct - TCP/UDP, global, HA | | C | Fragile, wrong protocol, CloudFront | | D | ALB + CloudFront breaks DNS |

choices.solution:
Attach Elastic IP addresses to the six EC2 instances. Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the six EC2 instances.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.
choices.explanation: CloudFront cannot accelerate the UDP and TCP DNS protocol used by these servers.

choices.solution:
Replace the two NLBs with two Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Create an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to route requests to one of the two ALBs.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.
choices.explanation: An Application Load Balancer handles HTTP-family traffic, not DNS over UDP or TCP; CloudFront does not resolve that limitation.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs its two-tier ecommerce website on AWS. The web tier consists of a load balancer that sends traffic to Amazon EC2 instances.

The database tier uses an Amazon RDS DB instance. The EC2 instances and the RDS DB instance should not be exposed to the public internet.

The EC2 instances require internet access to complete payment processing of orders through a third-party web service. The application must be highly available.

Which combination of configuration options will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in private subnets. Deploy an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance in private subnets.
choices.explanation: Private application instances behind the load balancer and a Multi-AZ RDS deployment provide application and database availability.

choices.solution: Configure a VPC with two private subnets and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the private subnets.
choices.explanation: An internal ALB cannot accept public customer traffic, and NAT gateways providing internet egress must be deployed in public subnets.

choices.solution: Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in public subnets across two Availability Zones. Deploy an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance in private subnets.
choices.explanation: Placing the application instances in public subnets does not meet the requested private web-tier placement.

choices.solution: Configure a VPC with one public subnet, one private subnet, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the public subnet.
choices.explanation: An Application Load Balancer requires subnets in at least two Availability Zones; a single public and single private subnet also cannot support the proposed two-AZ NAT design.

choices.solution: Configure a VPC with two public subnets, two private subnets, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets.
choices.explanation: An internet-facing ALB uses public subnets in two Availability Zones. A NAT gateway in each zone gives private application instances resilient outbound access to the payment service.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company wants to run applications in containers in the AWS Cloud. These applications are stateless and can tolerate disruptions within the underlying infrastructure.

The company needs a solution that minimizes cost and operational overhead.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Use Spot Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.
choices.explanation: An EC2 Auto Scaling group alone does not manage container scheduling and orchestration; those operations remain the company's responsibility.

choices.solution: Use Spot Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.
choices.explanation: An EKS managed node group manages Kubernetes worker lifecycle; Spot reduces cost for stateless, interruption-tolerant workloads. Use diverse instance types and handle interruptions.

choices.solution: Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.
choices.explanation: On-Demand instances cost more than Spot for disruption-tolerant containers and still require the company to operate the container platform.

choices.solution: Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.
choices.explanation: Managed nodes reduce operational work, but On-Demand pricing misses the Spot savings available for this interruption-tolerant workload.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer.

The application performs best when the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances is at or near 40%.

What should a solutions architect do to maintain the desired performance across all instances in the group?

choices.solution: Use a simple scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: Simple scaling requires manually configured alarms and adjustment sizes; it does not automatically maintain a specified average CPU target.

choices.solution: Use a target tracking policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: A target tracking policy scales the EC2 group to maintain the specified CPU target, rather than using fixed capacity or a schedule for changing demand.

choices.solution: Use an AWS Lambda function ta update the desired Auto Scaling group capacity.
choices.explanation: Custom Lambda capacity logic adds implementation and maintenance work when target tracking already maintains a 40% CPU target.

choices.solution: Use scheduled scaling actions to scale up and scale down the Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: Scheduled scaling follows a timetable rather than responding to actual CPU utilization.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company's website provides users with downloadable historical performance reports. The website needs a solution that will scale to meet the company's website demands globally.

The solution should be cost-effective, limit the provisioning of infrastructure resources, and provide the fastest possible response time.

Which combination should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Amazon CloudFront and Amazon S3
choices.explanation: S3 stores the downloadable reports and CloudFront caches them near users globally, reducing origin load and latency without maintaining web servers.

choices.solution: AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB
choices.explanation: Lambda and DynamoDB add execution and database components rather than caching downloadable report objects near global users.

choices.solution: Application Load Balancer with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
choices.explanation: EC2 Auto Scaling and an ALB require running compute and do not provide CloudFront's global edge caching for static reports.

choices.solution: Amazon Route 53 with internal Application Load Balancers
choices.explanation: Internal ALBs are not publicly accessible, and DNS routing does not cache reports at global edge locations.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs an Oracle database on premises. As part of the company's migration to AWS, the company wants to upgrade the database to the most recent available version.

The company also wants to set up disaster recovery (DR) for the database. The company needs to minimize the operational overhead for normal operations and DR setup.

The company also needs to maintain access to the database's underlying operating system.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Migrate the Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Set up database replication to a different AWS Region.
choices.explanation: EC2 provides OS access but requires the company to manage Oracle installation, upgrades, replication, and recovery.

choices.solution: Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Activate Cross-Region automated backups to replicate the snapshots to another AWS Region.
choices.explanation: Standard RDS for Oracle does not provide the OS-level access required for the upgrade customization.

choices.solution: Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle. Create a read replica for the database in another AWS Region.
choices.explanation: RDS Custom for Oracle allows supported operating-system and database customization. A cross-Region replica provides a recovery option with less administration than self-managed EC2 replication.

choices.solution: Migrate the Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Create a standby database in another Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: A Multi-AZ deployment does not grant OS access to standard RDS for Oracle.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company is migrating its on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The on-premises database must remain online and accessible during the migration.

The Aurora database must remain synchronized with the on-premises database.

Which combination of actions must a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

choices.solution: Create an ongoing replication task.
choices.explanation: A full-load and ongoing change-data-capture task keeps Aurora synchronized while the source database remains online.

choices.solution: Create a database backup of the on-premises database.
choices.explanation: A backup is a point-in-time copy and does not keep the target synchronized with subsequent source changes.

choices.solution: Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication server.
choices.explanation: A DMS replication instance connects to the source and target and performs the migration task.

choices.solution: Convert the database schema by using the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).
choices.explanation: Schema Conversion Tool converts database structures and code; it does not continuously replicate changing table data.

choices.solution: Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule to monitor the database synchronization.
choices.explanation: EventBridge routes events but does not implement database change-data capture and replication.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs its ecommerce application on AWS. Every new order is published as a message in a RabbitMQ queue that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance in a single Availability Zone.

These messages are processed by a different application that runs on a separate EC2 instance. This application stores the details in a PostgreSQL database on another EC2 instance.

All the EC2 instances are in the same Availability Zone. The company needs to redesign its architecture to provide the highest availability with the least operational overhead.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

choices.solution:
Migrate the queue to a redundant pair (active/standby) of RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application.

Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database.
choices.explanation: RabbitMQ on Amazon MQ uses a multi-AZ cluster deployment rather than ActiveMQ's active/standby model, and a DB Auto Scaling group does not configure database replication.

choices.solution:
Migrate the RabbitMQ queue to an Amazon MQ cluster deployment across three Availability Zones. Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for the application.

Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ enabled.
choices.explanation: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ uses a three-node Multi-AZ cluster for high availability, rather than the active/standby pair used for ActiveMQ. Multi-AZ application instances and RDS remove the remaining single-zone dependencies.

choices.solution:
Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application.

Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
choices.explanation: Auto Scaling EC2 brokers does not itself configure RabbitMQ clustering, replicated queues, or broker failover.

choices.solution:
Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the RabbitMQ queue. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the application.

Create a third Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database
choices.explanation: Auto Scaling groups do not automatically configure the stateful replication and failover required by RabbitMQ and PostgreSQL.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A reporting team receives files each day in an Amazon S3 bucket. The reporting team manually reviews and copies the files from this initial S3 bucket to an analysis S3 bucket each day at the same time to use with Amazon QuickSight.

Additional teams are starting to send more files in larger sizes to the initial S3 bucket. The reporting team wants to move the files automatically analysis S3 bucket as the files enter the initial S3 bucket.

The reporting team also wants to use AWS Lambda functions to run pattern-matching code on the copied data. In addition, the reporting team wants to send the data files to a pipeline in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.solution:
Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket.

Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.
choices.explanation: Custom copy code adds maintenance, and S3 event notifications cannot directly invoke SageMaker as a notification destination.

choices.solution:
Create a Lambda function to copy the files to the analysis S3 bucket. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).

Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.
choices.explanation: Maintaining a Lambda function to copy objects adds operational work that managed S3 replication avoids.

choices.solution:
Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Create an S3 event notification for the analysis S3 bucket.

Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as destinations of the event notification. Configure s3:ObjectCreated:Put as the event type.
choices.explanation: SageMaker is not a direct S3 event-notification destination; the proposed direct trigger cannot be configured.

choices.solution:
Configure S3 replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the analysis S3 bucket to send event notifications to Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events).

Configure an ObjectCreated rule in EventBridge (CloudWatch Events). Configure Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets for the rule.
choices.explanation:
Configure an EventBridge rule for the s3:ObjectCreated:Put event to invoke an AWS Lambda function for pattern-matching and to start the pipeline in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines. Explanation: S3 replication removes the need for a custom Lambda function to copy files (least operational overhead).

A plain S3 event notification can only target SNS, SQS, Lambda, or EventBridge directly - it cannot target SageMaker Pipelines. Routing through EventBridge is what lets a single ObjectCreated event fan out to both the pattern-matching Lambda function and the SageMaker Pipelines pipeline.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A company runs a web-based portal that provides users with global breaking news, local alerts, and weather updates. The portal delivers each user a personalized view by using mixture of static and dynamic content.

Content is served over HTTPS through an API server running on an Amazon EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company wants the portal to provide this content to its users across the world as quickly as possible.

How should a solutions architect design the application to ensure the LEAST amount of latency for all users?

choices.solution: Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve all static and dynamic content by specifying the ALB as an origin.
choices.explanation: CloudFront delivers static and dynamic HTTPS content through nearby edge locations and optimized origin connections. Use the ALB as the origin and configure cache policies so personalized responses are not shared between users.

choices.solution: Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
choices.explanation: Regional DNS routing selects an origin but does not cache content or provide CloudFront's edge-to-origin acceleration.

choices.solution:
Deploy the application stack in a single AWS Region. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the static content.

Serve the dynamic content directly from the ALB.
choices.explanation: Bypassing CloudFront for dynamic requests gives up its edge connection handling and optimized path to the origin.

choices.solution: Deploy the application stack in two AWS Regions. Use an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to serve all content from the ALB in the closest Region.
choices.explanation: Geolocation DNS routing does not provide global content caching or the same request acceleration as CloudFront.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
A gaming company is designing a highly available architecture. The application runs on a modified Linux kernel and supports only UDP-based traffic.

The company needs the front-end tier to provide the best possible user experience. That tier must have low latency, route traffic to the nearest edge location, and provide static IP addresses for entry into the application endpoints.

What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

choices.solution: Configure Amazon Route 53 to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in AWS Application Auto Scaling.
choices.explanation: An ALB does not support UDP, and Lambda does not provide control of a custom Linux kernel.

choices.solution: Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in an AWS Application Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: CloudFront does not proxy arbitrary UDP traffic, and Lambda cannot host the required modified operating system.

choices.solution: Configure AWS Global Accelerator to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: Global Accelerator supports UDP, static entry IPs, and regional failover. NLB distributes UDP traffic to EC2 instances that can run the modified Linux kernel.

choices.solution: Configure Amazon API Gateway to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
choices.explanation: API Gateway and an ALB do not expose the application's arbitrary UDP protocol.

Design Resilient Architectures.question:
